{{Short description|Modified stress-energy tensor in general relativity}}
In [[mathematical physics]], the '''Belinfante–Rosenfeld tensor''' is a modification of the [[stress–energy tensor]] that is constructed from the canonical stress–energy tensor and the spin current so as to be  symmetric yet still conserved. It is named after [[Frederik Belinfante]] and [[Léon Rosenfeld]] who published independently in 1940.<ref name="belinfante" /><ref name="rosenfeld" /> 

In a [[classical field theory|classical]] or [[quantum field theory|quantum]] [[local field]] theory, the generator of [[Lorentz transformation]]s  can be written as an integral

: <math>M_{\mu\nu} = \int \mathrm{d}^3x \, {M^0}_{\mu\nu}</math>

of a local current

: <math>{M^\mu}_{\nu\lambda}= (x_\nu {T^\mu}_\lambda - x_\lambda {T^\mu}_\nu)+ {S^\mu}_{\nu\lambda}.</math>

Here <math>{T^\mu}_\lambda</math> is the [[canonical stress–energy tensor]] satisfying <math>\partial_\mu {T^\mu}_{\lambda}=0</math>, and <math> {S^{\mu}}_{\nu\lambda}</math> is the contribution of the [[Relativistic angular momentum#Spin–orbital decomposition|intrinsic (spin) angular momentum]].  The anti-symmetry 
: <math>{M^\mu}_{\nu\lambda} = -{M^\mu}_{\lambda\nu}</math> 

implies the anti-symmetry 

: <math>{S^\mu}_{\nu\lambda} = -{S^\mu}_{\lambda\nu}.</math> 

Local conservation of angular momentum

: <math>\partial_\mu {M^\mu}_{\nu\lambda}=0 \, </math>

requires that

: <math>\partial_\mu {S^\mu}_{\nu\lambda}=T_{\lambda\nu}-T_{\nu\lambda}.</math>

Thus a source of [[spin tensor|spin-current]] implies a non-symmetric canonical stress–energy tensor.

The Belinfante–Rosenfeld tensor<ref name="belinfante">{{cite journal|author=F. J. Belinfante|title=On the current and the density of the electric charge, the energy, the linear momentum and the angular momentum of arbitrary fields |journal=Physica |volume=7|issue=5 | page=449| year=1940|doi=10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90091-X|bibcode=1940Phy.....7..449B|citeseerx=10.1.1.205.8093 }}</ref><ref name="rosenfeld">{{cite journal|author=L. Rosenfeld |title=Sur le tenseur d'impulsion-énergie |journal= Mémoires Acad. Roy. De Belgique |volume=18 |issue =6|pages= 1–30 |year=1940|url= http://neo-classical-physics.info/uploads/3/4/3/6/34363841/rosenfeld_-_on_the_energy-momentum_tensor.pdf}}</ref> is a modification of the stress–energy tensor

: <math>T_B^{\mu\nu} = T^{\mu\nu} +\frac 12 \partial_\lambda(S^{\mu\nu\lambda}+S^{\nu\mu\lambda}-S^{\lambda\nu\mu})</math>

that is constructed from the canonical stress–energy tensor and the spin current <math> {S^{\mu}}_{\nu\lambda}</math> so as to be  symmetric yet still conserved, i.e., 

: <math>\partial_\mu T_B^{\mu\nu} = 0.</math>
  
An [[integration by parts]] shows that

: <math>M^{\nu\lambda} = \int (x^\nu T^{0\lambda}_B - x^\lambda T^{0\nu}_B) \, \mathrm{d}^3x,</math>

and so a physical interpretation of Belinfante tensor is that it includes the "bound momentum" associated with gradients of the intrinsic angular momentum. In other words, the added term is an analogue of the <math> {\mathbf J}_\text{bound}= \nabla\times \mathbf {M}</math> "[[bound current]]" associated with a magnetization density <math>{\mathbf M}</math>.

The curious combination of spin-current components required to make <math> T_B^{\mu\nu}</math> symmetric and yet still conserved seems totally ''ad hoc'', but it was shown by both Rosenfeld and Belinfante that the modified tensor is precisely the symmetric Hilbert stress–energy tensor that acts as the source of gravity in  [[general relativity]].  Just as it is the sum of the bound and free currents that acts as a source of the magnetic field, it is the sum of the bound and free energy–momentum that acts as a source of gravity.

==Belinfante–Rosenfeld and the Hilbert energy–momentum tensor==

The Hilbert energy–momentum tensor <math>T_{\mu\nu}</math> is defined by the variation of the action functional <math>S_{\rm eff}</math> with respect to the metric as

:<math>\delta S_{\rm eff}=\frac 12 \int d^nx \sqrt{g} \,T_{\mu\nu}\,\delta g^{\mu\nu},</math>

or equivalently as

:<math>\delta S_{\rm eff}=-\frac 12 \int d^nx \sqrt{g} \,T^{\mu\nu}\,\delta g_{\mu\nu}. </math>

(The minus sign in the second equation arises because <math> \delta g^{\mu\nu}= - g^{\mu\sigma} \delta g_{\sigma\tau} g^{\tau\nu}</math> because <math>\delta(g^{\mu\sigma}g_{\sigma\tau})=0.</math>)

We may also define an energy–momentum tensor <math>T_{cb}</math> by varying a Minkowski-orthonormal [[vierbein]] <math> {\bf e}_a</math> to get

:<math> \delta S_{\rm eff}=  \int d^nx\sqrt{g}\left( \frac{\delta S}{\delta e^\mu_a}\right) \delta e^\mu_a  \equiv  \int d^nx\sqrt{g} \left(T_{cb} \eta^{ca} e^{*b}_\mu\right) \delta e^\mu_a.</math>

Here <math> \eta_{ab} = {\bf e}_a \cdot {\bf e}_b </math> is the Minkowski metric for the orthonormal vierbein frame, and <math>{\bf e}^{*b}</math> are the covectors dual to the vierbeins.

With the vierbein variation there is no immediately obvious  reason for <math>T_{cb}</math> to be symmetric. 
However, the  action functional <math> S_{\rm eff}({\bf e}_a) </math> should be invariant under  an [[infinitesimal]] local Lorentz transformation  <math>\delta e^\mu_a= e^\mu_b {\theta^{b}}_a(x)</math>, <math>\theta^{ab}=-\theta^{ba}</math>,
and so

:<math>\delta S_{\rm eff}
=   \int d^nx\sqrt{g} \,T_{cb}\,\eta^{ca} e^{*b}_\mu e^\mu_d {\theta^d}_a
=  \int d^nx\sqrt{g} \,T_{cb}\,\eta^{ca}  {\theta^b}_a
=  \int d^nx\sqrt{g}\, T_{cb}\, \theta^{bc}(x),
</math>

should be zero.
As  <math>\theta^{bc}(x)</math> is an arbitrary position-dependent skew [[symmetric matrix]], we see that local Lorentz and rotation invariance both requires and implies that <math>T_{bc}=T_{cb}</math>.

Once we know that <math>T_{ab}</math> is symmetric, it is easy to show that <math>T_{ab}= e_a^\mu e_b^\nu T_{\mu\nu}</math>, and so the vierbein-variation energy–momentum tensor is equivalent to the metric-variation Hilbert tensor.

We can now understand  the origin of the Belinfante–Rosenfeld modification of the Noether canonical energy momentum tensor. 
Take the  action to be  <math>S_{\rm eff}({\bf e}_a, {\omega}^{ab}_\mu )</math> where   <math>{\omega}^{ab}_\mu</math> is the [[spin connection]] that is   determined by <math>{\bf e}_a</math> via the condition of being metric compatible and torsion free.  The spin current <math>{S^\mu}_{ab}</math>  is then   defined by the variation

:<math>
{S^\mu}_{ab}= \frac{2}{\sqrt g} \left.\left(\frac{\delta S_{\rm eff}}{\delta \omega^{ab}_\mu}\right)\right|_{{\bf e}_a}
</math>

the vertical bar denoting that the <math>{\bf e}_a</math> are held fixed during the variation. The "canonical" Noether energy momentum tensor <math>T^{(0)}_{cb}</math>  is the part that arises from the variation where we keep the spin connection fixed:

:<math>
 T_{cb} ^{(0)}  \eta^{ca} e^{*b}_\mu= \frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\left.\left(\frac{\delta S_{\rm eff}}{\delta e^\mu_a}\right)\right|_{\omega^{ab}_\mu}.
</math>

Then

:<math>
\delta S_{\rm eff} = \int d^nx \sqrt{g} \left\{ T_{cb} ^{(0)}  \eta^{ca} e^{*b}_\mu  \delta e^\mu_a+ \frac 12 {S^{\mu}}_{ab} \delta {\omega^{ab}}_\mu\right\}.
</math>

Now, for a torsion-free and metric-compatible connection, we have
that

:<math>
(\delta \omega_{ij\mu}) e^\mu_k 
=-\frac 12\left\{(\nabla_j \delta e_{ik} -  \nabla_k  \delta e_{ij})
+( \nabla_k \delta e_{ji}- \nabla_i  \delta e_{jk}) -( \nabla_i \delta e_{kj}-\nabla_j \delta e_{ki})\right\},
</math>

where we are using the notation

:<math>
\delta e_{ij} =  {\bf e}_i\cdot \delta {\bf e}_j= \eta_{ib}[e^{*b}_\alpha \delta e_j^\alpha].
</math>

Using the spin-connection variation, and after an integration by parts, we find

:<math>
\delta S_{\rm eff} = \int d^nx \sqrt{g} \left\{ T_{cb} ^{(0)} +\frac 12 \nabla_a({S_{bc}}^a+{S_{cb}}^a-{S^a}_{bc})\right\}  \eta^{cd}e^{*b}_\mu \,\delta e_d^\mu.
</math>

Thus we see that  corrections to the canonical Noether tensor that appear in the  Belinfante–Rosenfeld tensor occur because we need to simultaneously vary the vierbein and the spin connection if we are to preserve local Lorentz invariance.

As an example,  consider the  classical Lagrangian for the Dirac field

:<math>
\int d^dx\sqrt{g}\left\{ \frac i 2 \left( \bar \Psi \gamma^a e^\mu_a\nabla_\mu \Psi - (\nabla_\mu \bar\Psi)e^\mu_a \gamma^a \Psi\right)+m\bar\Psi\Psi \right\}.
</math>

Here the [[spinor]] covariant derivatives are

:<math>
\nabla_\mu \Psi =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}+\frac 18 [\gamma_b,\gamma_c] {\omega^{bc}}_\mu\right) \Psi,
</math>

:<math>
\nabla_\mu\bar  \Psi =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}-\frac 18 [\gamma_b,\gamma_c] {\omega^{bc}}_\mu\right) \bar\Psi.
</math>

We therefore get

:<math>
T^{(0)}_{bc}= \frac i2\left(\bar \Psi \gamma_c( \nabla_b\Psi) -(\nabla_b \bar \Psi)\gamma_c \Psi\right),
</math>

:<math>
{S^a}_{bc}= \frac i8 \bar\Psi\{\gamma^a,[\gamma_b,\gamma_c]\}\Psi.
</math>

There is no contribution from <math>\sqrt{g}</math> if we use the equations of motion, i.e. we are on shell.

Now  
:<math>
\{\gamma_a,[\gamma_b,\gamma_c]\}=4 \gamma_a\gamma_b\gamma_c, 
</math>
if <math>a, b, c</math> are distinct 
and zero otherwise.
As a consequence  <math>S_{abc}</math>  is totally anti-symmetric. Now,  using this result, and again  the equations of motion, we find that

:<math>
\nabla_a {S^a}_{bc}= T^{(0)}_{cb}-T^{(0)}_{bc}.
</math>

Thus  the Belinfante–Rosenfeld  tensor becomes

:<math>
T_{bc} = T^{(0)}_{bc}+ \frac 12(T^{(0)}_{cb}-T^{(0)}_{bc})
= \frac 12 (T^{(0)}_{bc}+T^{(0)}_{cb}).
</math>

The  Belinfante–Rosenfeld  tensor for the Dirac field is  therefore seen to be  the symmetrized canonical energy–momentum tensor.

==Weinberg's definition==

[[Steven Weinberg]] defined the Belinfante tensor as<ref>{{cite book|last1=Weinberg|first1=Steven|title=The quantum theory of fields|date=2005|publisher=[[Cambridge Univ. Press]]|location=Cambridge [u.a.]|isbn=9780521670531|edition=Repr., pbk.}}</ref>
:<math>T_B^{\mu\nu}=T^{\mu\nu}-\frac{i}{2}\partial_\kappa \left[\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\kappa\Psi^\ell)}(\mathcal{J}^{\mu\nu})^\ell_{\,\, m}\Psi^m-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\Psi^\ell)}(\mathcal{J}^{\kappa\nu})^\ell_{\,\, m}\Psi^m-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\nu\Psi^\ell)}(\mathcal{J}^{\kappa\mu})^\ell_{\,\, m}\Psi^m\right]    </math>
where <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is the [[Lagrangian density]], the set {Ψ} are the fields appearing in the Lagrangian, the non-Belinfante energy momentum tensor is defined by
:<math>T^{\mu\nu}=\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal{L}-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\Psi^\ell)}\partial^\nu\Psi^\ell</math>
and <math>\mathcal{J^{\mu\nu}}</math> are a set of matrices satisfying the algebra of the homogeneous [[Lorentz group]]<ref>{{cite book|last1=Cahill|first1=Kevin, [[University of New Mexico]]|title=Physical mathematics|date=2013|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|location=Cambridge|isbn=9781107005211|edition=Repr.}}</ref>
:<math>[\mathcal{J}^{\mu\nu},\mathcal{J}^{\rho\sigma}]=i\mathcal{J}^{\nu\rho}\eta^{\mu\sigma}-i\mathcal{J}^{\nu\sigma}\eta^{\mu\rho}-i\mathcal{J}^{\mu\rho}\eta^{\nu\sigma}+i\mathcal{J}^{\mu\sigma}\eta^{\nu\rho}</math>.
